newsitem.title: GERMANY: Copper backwardation seen partly backed by tightness.
newsitem.headline: Copper backwardation seen partly backed by tightness.

text.p: The expanding copper backwardation on the London Metals Exchange (LME) is partly based on tight nearby supplies, said Juergen Hartmann, board spokesman at German copper plant Huettenwerke Kayser AG.

"There is strong physical demand while supply is relatively limited," he said in response to questions during a news conference organised by metals trade association VDM here. Hartmann added a certain amount of speculation also seemed involved.
The LME cash to three months backwardation spread, which has strengthened sharply during the week, was last just below $200.

Hartmann said in contrast to the tight nearby situation, copper markets at the end of 1997 should be balanced. Supply additions were well publicised and would exceed demand growth over the next few years.

He said separately that former Soviet Union supply of aluminium, nickel and copper was freely flowing into the western world as domestic military industries had drastically reduced their metals intake.
"Without this factor, we would see sharply higher metals prices," he said. Lead and zinc exports to the West were more restricted because Kazakhstan was increasing its domestic consumption.
